title: Emergency Myelopoiesis in the Control of Blood Production
text:
Disruption of mechanisms regulating emergency myelopoiesis (EM) pathways, in particular in response
to inflammatory triggers, has significant detrimental consequences for the organism across many life stages and
disease contexts, making EM pathways prime mechanisms to target for translational applications. A major barrier
in turning these findings into therapeutic strategies is our lack of understanding of EM pathways contributions to
many pathophysiological situations. Our research project seeks to remove this roadblock by investigating the
contribution of EM pathways to adaptive and maladaptive myelopoiesis associated with immune deregulations,
solid cancers, and blood disorders.

title: Macrophages and fibroblasts in the progression of lung cancer
text:
While treatments like immunotherapy have improved, late-stage patients often don’t respond well. Few
therapies target macrophages and fibroblasts within the tumor, despite evidence suggesting these cell
types contribute to tumor progression. This K00 project will use in vivo gene editing of macrophages and
fibroblasts to identify immune suppressive phenotypes and pathways contributing to lung cancer tumor
progression.

title: A Novel Open-Source Optimization Framework for the Design and Simulation of Radiofrequency Coils for Magnetic Resonance Imaging
text:
The goal of this project is to develop and demonstrate a novel shape optimization approach for the design of
radiofrequency coils based on ultimate performance benchmarks. This project will introduce a new method for
rational coil design that relies on rapid volume-surface integral equation techniques to simulate the coils’
radiofrequency fields and advanced shape modeling algorithms to automatically explore geometric variations
and find the optimal design. The proposed coil design optimization framework will be validated in simulations
and experiments, and released as open-source with potential applications beyond MRI.

title: Decoy Adhesion by Veillonella atypica: Hag1-Mediated Shielding of Oral Epithelium from Porphyromonas gingivalis - Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential
text:
Periodontal disease affects millions worldwide and arises from polymicrobial dysbiosis driven by the keystone
pathogen Porphyromonas gingivalis. This R21 will define how the commensal Veillonella atypica – focusing on
its giant adhesin Hag1 and domain-specific interactions with oral epithelial cells and P. gingivalis – modulates
colonization and host inflammatory responses. Elucidating these mechanisms could enable adhesin-based or
probiotic strategies to block P. gingivalis colonization, offering innovative preventative or therapeutic approaches
to improve oral and systemic health.

title: The Impact of TrpA1/TrpV1 activity on the Ocular Mucinome
text:
Bacterial corneal infections are sight-threatening, cost the USA an estimated $175 million in annual direct health
expenditures (2010 estimates), and are becoming increasingly difficult to combat due to the global antimicrobial
resistance crisis. Previously, the Fleiszig group discovered that ocular mucins and a family of sensory nerve-
associated ion channels both function to protect the cornea against bacterial adhesion, the latter displaying
specificity for pathogen type (i.e. TRPA1 against P. aeruginosa, and TRPV1 against S. aureus) Here, I will test
the hypothesis that the two nerve associated channel types differentially modulate mucin expression using novel
methods that enable unprecedented detail, thereby improving our understanding of the ocular surface mucinome
and its regulation during health, which could ultimately lead to novel mucin-based strategies for protecting
against sight-threatening eye infections and possibly also life-threatening infections caused by the same
pathogens in other mucosal systems.

title: Epigenetics, DNA repair and Genomics (EDGe) Training Program in Cancer
text: A steady stream of new researchers is necessary to continue the fight against cancer, one of the primary causes of death in the U.S. To achieve this goal, it is critical that we train the next generation of scientists in state-of-the-art cancer research; this is a key aspect of this proposed training program. The goal of this Epigenetic, DNA repair and Genomics (EDGe) Training Program in Cancer is to train 4 Ph.D. students per year in multidisciplinary cancer research building on our institutional faculty's strength in DNA repair and epigenetics - key areas that impact cancer development and treatment.

title: Computational Analysis of Enzyme Catalysis and Regulation
text:
The multi-faceted computational methodologies we develop will be applicable to a broad set
of metalloenzymes and proteins of biomedical importance. We target fundamental mechanistic problems in
enzymes that catalyze phosphoryl transfer reactions, since mutations in these enzymes are implicated in nu-
merous human diseases such as cancer, insulin resistance and diabetes; abnormal cysteine dioxygenase
activity is also linked to many human diseases, including autoimmunity, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's dis-
ease, rheumatoid arthritis, and motor neuron diseases. Although our project does not focus on design of
drugs, the mechanistic insights into enzyme catalysis and allosteric regulation will broaden strategies that can
be used to target various systems of biomedical signiﬁcance.

title: Mechanistic Elucidation of Mitochondrial Stress Response in Human Cells
text:
Mitochondrial dysfunction is closely linked to a spectrum of disorders, ranging from primary
mitochondrial diseases to age-associated conditions like neurodegenerative diseases. The
proposed work here seeks to comprehensively uncover the intricate molecular mechanisms
governing the maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis. These findings hold significant promise
for unlocking potential therapeutic avenues to treat diseases associated with mitochondrial
dysfunction.

title: Identifying novel small molecule molting regulators for anthelmintic drug development
text:
Parasitic nematodes infect over a billion people worldwide, and there is an urgent need for new therapeutic
targets to combat rising drug resistance to current treatments. Molting, a biological process fundamental to
nematode development, is an attractive anti-parasitic drug target, but there is a gap in knowledge of how small
molecule signals can regulate molting. I aim to identify the first known small molecule regulators of molting,
advancing our understanding of the biology of molting across nematodes and developing molting as a feasible
anti-parasitic drug target for future drug development efforts.

title: The evolution and diversity of mutation, molecular fidelity, and genome structure
text:
The structure and sequence of genomes is shaped by the forces of mutation, selection, and drift acting in the
context of different life histories and environments. Over evolutionary timescales, changes to genome structure and
content are associated with vast phenotypic changes between and within species, while throughout the lifetime of
an organism individual cells accumulate somatic mutations and germ cells accumulate damage and lesions that are
passed down to progeny. We seek to understand the processes that guide these changes to genomes across
different timescales.

title: Targeting nutrient microenvironment imprinted therapy resistance in pancreatic cancer
text:
The tumor microenvironment of pancreatic adenocarcinomas endows these tumors with profound resistance to
chemotherapies, which severely hinders clinical management of this disease. We have found that nutrient
availability in pancreatic tumors is a key microenvironmental factor that leads to this therapy resistance. In this
proposal, we will determine the molecular mechanisms by which tumor nutrition imparts therapy resistance upon
pancreatic cancer cells, and if manipulating tumor nutrition and its impact on pancreatic cancer cells can sensitize
pancreatic tumors to chemotherapies, which may lead to new therapeutic approaches in this disease.

title: Dissecting metabolic functions of mitochondrial electron transport in kidney epithelium
text:
The kidney relies on mitochondria, the cell’s powerhouses, to generate the
energy required for ion, solute, and water transport. Impaired mitochondrial function not only disrupts
these processes but also leads to kidney injury and inflammation. This project will define the role of
mitochondrial electron transport in the regulation of kidney epithelial cell metabolism and signaling and
aims to identify new therapeutic targets that mitigate the consequences of mitochondrial dysfunction in
the kidney.

title: Optimization of a single cell multi-omic analysis platform for circulating and therapeutic immune cells
text:
We propose further optimization and application of a new single cell multi-omics platform that
allows thousands of single immune cells to be captured, localized, visualized and serially
analyzed by MALDI mass spectrometry to sequentially detect multiple analytes. Analysis
workflows will be standardized for analysis of metabolites, lipids, glycans and proteins in
peripheral blood mononuclear cell preparations undergoing differentiation and from clinical
therapeutic preparations of CAR-T cells targeting cancers.

title: A Transformative Structural Proteomics Platform for Early Detection of Misfolding-Driven Cardiovascular Diseases
text:
This project will develop a first-in-class blood test platform for the minimally invasive detection of
misfolded proteins, a key driver of numerous life-threatening heart and blood diseases such as
transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy and unexplained heart failure, that affect millions of people
in the U.S. yet remain largely undetectable by conventional diagnostic methods due to a lack of
molecular tools. By enabling the direct and importantly, pre-symptomatic detection of misfolding
events in just 10 µl of plasma, our novel platform technology has the potential to accurately
diagnose previously hard-to-detect conditions, prevent or reverse disease progression, and shift
fatal diseases into manageable chronic conditions. Its broader application to other misfolding-
related disorders may transform how heart, lung, blood, and sleep diseases are detected and
managed, greatly improving treatment outcomes.

title: Global proteomics mass spectrometry data sharing infrastructure
text:
Global proteomics mass spectrometry data sharing infrastructure – Project Narrative
Mass spectrometry based proteomics is a key technology for the identification and quantification of proteins in
many types of biological samples, which can be used to determine how abundances of proteins are affected by
perturbed cellular systems under stress or the cause of a disease. We propose a substantial advancement of
proteomics mass spectrometry data repository resources to enable researchers to share, find, access, and reuse
proteomics datasets at a global scale.

title: Unraveling the genetic basis of cellular behaviors with deep learning and imaging-based reverse genetics
text:
Modern imaging technologies now allow us to measure the spatial, temporal, and genomic axes
of variation in living systems; as such, it is now possible for images to be a universal data type
for the life sciences. This proposal seeks to make this vision reality by developing new
computational methods for characterizing the behavior of single cells in biological images and
creating a new experimental approach to imaging-based reverse genetics. The proposed work
will make spatial genomics methods accessible to users of all skill levels and empower a new
generation of multi-modal single cell measurements – advances that will drive broad and
sustained impact throughout the scientific community.

title: Decoding the Genetic and Epigenetic Mechanisms of Bifunctional Cis-Regulatory Elements
text:
Bifunctional cis-regulatory elements (CREs) can drive distinct biological processes by acting as enhancers in
one cell type, but as silencers in another. However, we still do not understand the cellular, genetic, and epigenetic
contexts that confer bifunctional CRE activity across different cell types or developmental stages. Our findings
will help us understand how DNA sequence and cell-type-specific epigenetic states drive bifunctional CRE
activity.

title: Clinical context of SuicIde following OPIOID transitionS in Veterans, CSI:OPIOIDS-V
text:
Opioid prescribing has fallen across the US, both within and outside the US Veterans Administration. Although
this change likely will prevent prescription-related harm for a number of patients, reports signal adverse events
including suicide, for others. Where harm has occurred, it is crucial to know what factors, modifiable and
nonmodifiable, played a role. Whereas much research has sought statistical associations between prescription
opioid change and outcomes like suicide, we offer a different approach. We will recruit bereaved survivors of
suicides following a prescription opioid change. We will carry out detailed survey, medical record review, and
in-depth psychological autopsy interviews to learn which patient and clinical context factors could help to
account for why the suicides took place. This research is descriptive. The research team includes scholarly
experts and members of the affected communities. Working with VA partners, we seek actionable points of
leverage for policy makers, and for health systems seeking to prevent these suicides from taking place.

title: Structural Dynamics of Viral Proteins: Development and Application of Multiscale Computational Methods for Studying Viral Capsids, Proteins and Membrane Systems
text:
This project will use computational methods to characterize molecular details of viral infection processes in
enteroviruses, which include severe pathogens EV-A71 and EV-D68. Children are most susceptible to these
viruses, which can cause severe respiratory symptoms, paralysis and can even be fatal, and at the current time
there are no approved treatments for these viral infections. This project will provide fundamental knowledge
about the enterovirus infection process, which can lead to new drug development strategies against these
pathogens.

title: Role of human NK cells in the immune response to Coccidioides
text:
Coccidioides is a dimorphic fungus endemic to the United States with a geographical distribution 
that is rapidly expanding, and which can cause mild lung disease or severe disseminated 
disease. The proposed studies will dissect the human innate immune response to Coccidioides 
with a focus on natural killer (NK) cells, through spatial analysis of patient granulomas, 
mechanistic studies of NK cell/fungus interactions, patient cohort immune profiling, and human 
airway infection models. Successful completion of the proposed Aims will reveal mechanisms of 
Coccidioides pathogenesis and host defense and point the way to new treatments for severe 
disease and methods for the study of fungal pathogenesis.
